paper_context.research_question: How can the benefits of Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and attention-based mechanisms be jointly utilized in an end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system to improve performance, simplify the model-building process, and address alignment issues without relying on extensive linguistic resources?
main_claims: The proposed joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR effectively combines the advantages of CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient computation) and attention (no conditional independence assumptions) during both training and decoding.
This joint approach addresses the irregular alignment issues (deletion/insertion errors) inherent in pure attention-based ASR.

The method significantly simplifies the ASR model-building process by eliminating the need for linguistic resources (e.g., pronunciation dictionaries, morphological analyzers, word segmentation) and complex module-specific processes.

The joint CTC-attention system achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases superior to, state-of-the-art conventional hybrid ASR systems on spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) benchmarks.
The joint decoding strategy simplifies the inference step by reducing the need for extensive parameter tuning (e.g., length penalties, coverage terms) compared to attention-only decoding.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Character Error Rate (CER) on ASR benchmarks
Effectiveness in mitigating irregular alignments (deletion/insertion errors)
Degree of simplification in the ASR model-building and decoding process
Generalizability across different languages and speech characteristics
Comparison against state-of-the-art hybrid and end-to-end ASR systems
Robustness to hyperparameter tuning (e.g., λ in joint decoding)

supporting_evidence: The main reason for choosing these two languages is that those ideogram languages have relatively shorter lengths for letter sequences than those in alphabet languages, which reduces computational complexities greatly, and makes it easy to handle context information in a decoder network.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR system, aiming to combine the strengths of both CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient computation) and attention mechanisms (no conditional independence assumptions) while addressing their individual weaknesses. The core argument is structured around solving the complexity and resource dependency of conventional hybrid ASR, and the alignment issues of pure attention-based ASR. The proposed solution involves multi-task learning for training (CTC as a regularization objective) and a two-pass rescoring technique for decoding. The paper then empirically validates this approach on spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) benchmarks, demonstrating comparable or superior performance to conventional hybrid systems without linguistic resources, and significant simplification of the ASR building and decoding process. The logical flow is clear, moving from problem identification to proposed solution, detailed mechanism, empirical validation, and discussion of benefits and future work.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Conventional ASR systems are complex, module-based, rely on linguistic resources, make conditional independence assumptions, and suffer from local optima and complex decoding (Section 1).

P2: End-to-end ASR aims to simplify this, with two main types: attention-based (flexible, no independence assumptions, but prone to irregular alignments) and CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient, but requires language models/graph-based decoding) (Section 1, 2).
S1: Propose a joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR system to combine benefits and mitigate weaknesses (C1, Section 1).

M1: During training, use multi-task learning (MTL) where a CTC objective regularizes the attention-based encoder, enforcing monotonic alignment and speeding up alignment estimation (C3, C4, C6, C7, Section 3.1).

M2: During decoding, implement a two-pass rescoring technique where CTC probabilities enforce monotonic alignment, preventing irregular alignments (jumps/loops) and simplifying parameter tuning (C5, C8, C9, Section 3.2).
E1: Experiments on CSJ show MTL significantly outperforms attention-only ASR, and joint decoding further improves performance (C11, C12, Section 4.1).
E2: Performance on CSJ is not highly sensitive to the re-scoring weight parameter λ (C13, Section 4.1).
E3: The proposed method achieves comparable state-of-the-art performance on CSJ without linguistic resources (C14, Section 4.1).

E4: Experiments on MTS show MTL and joint decoding significantly improve performance over attention-only, achieving competitive results against moderate SOTA systems without linguistic resources (C11, C12, C15, Section 4.2).
C3: The proposed method greatly simplifies the ASR building process by eliminating GMM-HMM, DNN pre-training, lattice generation, and complex decoding search (C16, Section 5).
C4: The training time is comparable to conventional SOTA systems due to this simplification (C17, Section 5).
C5: The method achieves comparable/superior performance to SOTA conventional hybrid ASR on CSJ and MTS without linguistic resources (C2, Section 5).
L1: Scalability to languages with long sequence lengths (e.g., English) remains a challenge for future work (U1, A3, Section 5).
A1: Ideogram languages simplify computational complexities and context handling due to shorter letter sequences (A1, Section 4).
A2: Top-tier SOTA hybrid systems leverage linguistic knowledge (phoneme representation) which is hard to beat without such knowledge (A2, Section 4.2).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a joint CTC-attention end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system designed to combine the strengths of Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) for monotonic alignment and attention mechanisms for their lack of conditional independence assumptions. The core methodological innovation lies in a multi-task learning (MTL) framework for training, where a shared encoder is simultaneously optimized by both CTC and attention objectives. This is intended to regularize the attention mechanism, guiding it towards more monotonic alignments and mitigating issues like deletion and insertion errors prevalent in pure attention-based models. For decoding, a two-pass rescoring strategy is introduced, where initial attention-based hypotheses are refined using a weighted combination of attention and CTC probabilities. This joint decoding aims to simplify the inference process by reducing the need for extensive parameter tuning (e.g., length penalties, coverage terms, min/max lengths). The method is empirically validated on spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) benchmarks, with a stated goal of achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art conventional hybrid ASR systems while significantly simplifying the model-building process by eliminating reliance on linguistic resources such as pronunciation dictionaries and morphological analyzers.
logical_argument_graph: Traditional ASR systems are complex, resource-intensive, and suffer from conditional independence assumptions and local optima (Section 1).

End-to-end ASR aims to simplify this, with two main types: attention-based (flexible, no independence assumptions, but prone to irregular alignments) and CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient, but requires LMs/graph-based decoding in some cases) (Section 1, 2.2, 2.3).

Hypothesis: Combining CTC and attention can leverage their respective strengths, specifically using CTC to regularize attention's alignment flexibility and simplify the overall ASR pipeline (Section 1, 3).

Methodological Proposal: Joint CTC-attention ASR with two components: (1) Multi-task learning (MTL) during training, using a shared encoder and a weighted sum of CTC and attention objectives (Section 3.1). (2) A two-pass joint decoding strategy that rescores attention-based hypotheses with CTC probabilities (Section 3.2).
Expected Outcomes: Reduced irregular alignments, simplified model building (no linguistic resources, fewer decoding parameters), and competitive performance (Section 1, 3.2, 5).
Empirical Validation: Experiments on CSJ and MTS datasets compare the proposed method against attention-only and conventional hybrid systems using Character Error Rate (CER) (Section 4).

Results: MTL and joint decoding improve performance over attention-only. The proposed method achieves comparable/superior CER to some SOTA hybrid systems on CSJ and MTS, without linguistic resources, and simplifies decoding parameter tuning (Section 4.1, 4.2, 5).
Conclusion: The joint CTC-attention approach effectively combines benefits, addresses alignment issues, simplifies ASR, and achieves competitive performance on ideogram languages (Section 5).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a joint Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC)-attention end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system. This approach incrementally refines existing attention-based ASR paradigms by integrating CTC's monotonic alignment properties during both training (via multi-task learning, inspired by prior work) and a novel two-pass decoding strategy. The core contribution is a meaningful simplification of the ASR model-building process, reducing the reliance on extensive linguistic resources and complex heuristic tuning, while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art conventional hybrid systems on spontaneous Japanese and Mandarin Chinese benchmarks. The work extends the utility of end-to-end ASR by mitigating irregular alignment issues inherent in pure attention models, making the system more robust and practical for certain language contexts.
logical_argument_graph: Conventional ASR systems are complex, resource-intensive, and suffer from conditional independence assumptions and local optima (Section 1).

End-to-end ASR aims to simplify this, with two main types: CTC (monotonic alignment, efficiency, but uses Markov assumptions) and attention (no conditional independence assumptions, flexible alignment, but prone to irregular alignments) (Section 1, 2).
Pure attention models suffer from irregular alignments (deletion/insertion errors) and require complex decoding parameter tuning (Section 2.3, 3.2).
The paper proposes a joint CTC-attention model to combine their benefits and mitigate attention's drawbacks (Section 1, 3).

During training, multi-task learning (MTL) uses a shared encoder with both CTC and attention objectives, where CTC acts as a regularizer to enforce monotonic alignment (Claim C1, C4, C6, C7) (Section 3.1), building on prior work by Kim et al. (2016).

During decoding, a two-pass rescoring technique integrates CTC probabilities with attention probabilities to refine hypotheses, enforcing monotonic alignment and reducing the need for extensive parameter tuning (Claim C1, C5, C8, C9) (Section 3.2).

Experiments are conducted on Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) ASR tasks (Section 4), chosen because ideogram languages have relatively shorter letter sequences, simplifying computational complexity (Assumption A1).
Experimental results demonstrate that MTL significantly outperforms attention-only ASR (Claim C11).
The proposed joint decoding strategy further improves performance beyond multi-task learning alone (Claim C12).
The joint CTC-attention system achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art conventional hybrid systems on CSJ and MTS, crucially without relying on linguistic resources (Claim C2, C14, C15).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system that jointly leverages Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and attention mechanisms. The core reasoning is to combine the strengths of both architectures: CTC's ability to enforce monotonic alignment and efficient computation, and attention's capacity to avoid conditional independence assumptions. This joint approach is applied during both training (via multi-task learning, where CTC acts as a regularizer for the attention encoder) and decoding (through a two-pass rescoring strategy that combines CTC and attention probabilities). The authors argue that this method effectively mitigates irregular alignment issues (deletion/insertion errors) common in pure attention-based ASR, while significantly simplifying the overall ASR model-building process by eliminating the need for extensive linguistic resources (e.g., pronunciation dictionaries, morphological analyzers) and complex heuristic parameter tuning in decoding. Empirical validation on spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) benchmarks demonstrates performance comparable to, and in some cases superior to, state-of-the-art conventional hybrid ASR systems, despite the reduced reliance on external resources.
logical_argument_graph: Traditional ASR systems are complex, require extensive linguistic resources, and suffer from conditional independence assumptions and local optima (Section 1).

End-to-end ASR aims to simplify this by using single-network architectures, with two main types: attention-based (flexible, no independence assumptions but prone to irregular alignments) and CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient but uses Markov assumptions) (Section 1, 2.2, 2.3).
Attention-based models' flexibility leads to irregular alignments (deletion/insertion errors) and requires complex decoding heuristics (length penalties, coverage terms) (Section 1, 3.2).
The paper proposes a joint CTC-attention approach to combine their benefits and address attention's weaknesses (Section 1, 3).
During training, multi-task learning uses a CTC objective to regularize the attention encoder, enforcing monotonic alignment and speeding up alignment estimation (Section 3.1).
During decoding, a two-pass rescoring technique combines CTC and attention probabilities, using CTC's monotonic property to guide alignment and simplify parameter tuning (Section 3.2).

Experiments on Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) show that this joint approach outperforms attention-only models and achieves comparable/superior performance to SOTA hybrid systems *without* linguistic resources (Section 4, 5).
The method thus simplifies the ASR building process, reduces resource dependency, and maintains competitive performance, even offering comparable training times due to simplification (Section 5).

logical_argument_graph: Conventional ASR systems are complex, resource-intensive (linguistic knowledge), and suffer from conditional independence assumptions, complex decoding, and local optima (Section 1).
End-to-end ASR aims to simplify this, with two main types: attention-based and CTC (Section 1).
Attention-based ASR avoids conditional independence assumptions but suffers from irregular alignments (deletion/insertion errors) due to its flexibility (Section 1, 2.3).
CTC enforces monotonic alignment and allows efficient computation but traditionally requires language models and graph-based decoding (Section 1, 2.2).
Proposed Solution: Joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR (Section 3).

Training: Multi-task learning (MTL) where a shared encoder is optimized by both CTC and attention objectives. CTC acts as a regularizer, enforcing monotonic alignment and speeding up alignment estimation during training (Section 3.1).

Decoding: Two-pass rescoring technique. First pass generates hypotheses using attention, second pass refines them using a weighted combination of attention and CTC probabilities. CTC probability enforces monotonic alignment, reducing the need for length penalties and coverage terms (Section 3.2).

Hypothesis: This joint approach will address irregular alignments, simplify the ASR building/decoding process (no linguistic resources, fewer tuning parameters), and achieve competitive performance (Section 1, 5).
Empirical Validation: Experiments on CSJ and MTS benchmarks (Section 4).
Results: MTL and joint decoding consistently outperform attention-only ASR (Tables 1 & 2).
Simplification: Joint decoding eliminates the need for length penalties, coverage terms, and min/max length tuning (Section 4.1, 4.2).
Performance: Achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases superior to, conventional hybrid SOTA systems on CSJ and MTS, without linguistic resources (Tables 1 & 2, Section 5).
Robustness: Performance is not highly sensitive to the λ parameter in joint decoding for CSJ (Figure 2).
Efficiency: Training time is comparable to conventional SOTA due to simplification (Section 5).

Conclusion: The proposed method effectively combines CTC and attention, simplifies ASR, and achieves competitive performance, though generalizability to long sequence languages like English needs further work (Section 5).

Summary: The paper proposes a joint CTC-attention end-to-end ASR system that effectively integrates the benefits of both CTC (monotonic alignment, efficient computation) and attention mechanisms (no conditional independence assumptions) during training and decoding. This approach significantly mitigates irregular alignment issues, simplifies the ASR model-building process by reducing reliance on linguistic resources and complex heuristic tuning, and achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art conventional hybrid systems on spontaneous Japanese and Mandarin Chinese benchmarks.

Strengths:
*   Effective integration of CTC and attention mechanisms to leverage their respective benefits and mitigate individual weaknesses, particularly addressing irregular alignments in attention-based models.
*   Significant simplification of the ASR model-building process by eliminating the need for extensive linguistic resources and complex module-specific components (e.g., GMM-HMMs, lattice generation).
*   The proposed joint decoding strategy simplifies the inference step by reducing the need for extensive heuristic parameter tuning (e.g., length penalties, coverage terms).
*   Achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases superior to, state-of-the-art conventional hybrid ASR systems on spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) and Mandarin Chinese (MTS) benchmarks, crucially without relying on linguistic resources.

Limitations:
*   The generalizability and efficiency of the proposed method for languages with significantly longer output sequence lengths (e.g., English) remain an open problem, as the current validation is focused on ideogram languages whose characteristics simplify computational complexities (Section 4, Section 5).
*   Direct comparison to some state-of-the-art reference systems is difficult due to acknowledged differences in training data amounts and experimental configurations, making the 'comparable performance' claim nuanced and not universally verifiable against all top-tier systems (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
*   The robustness of the re-scoring weight parameter λ was not fully demonstrated for the MTS dataset, as a sensitivity analysis similar to CSJ was not provided, raising questions about its task-dependency and potential need for tuning (Section 4.2).

Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
